summary: Children aged 9–11 move from 'the heart pumps blood' to the double-loop circulatory system: a four-chambered pump (two atria receive, two ventricles push) driving one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen and one loop to the body to deliver it, through arteries (away from heart, high pressure), veins (back to heart, with valves) and capillaries (walls one cell thick, where exchange happens). Blood is a mixture — red cells (oxygen), white cells (fight infection), platelets (clotting) and plasma. Teach it as a JOURNEY a drop of blood takes, tracing the circuit repeatedly until the double loop and its purpose become obvious: blood reloads oxygen at the lungs, comes back to the heart to be pumped out again, and unloads oxygen at the body. Ground vessel types in things children can feel: the wrist/neck pulse is an artery; the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand are veins. A driveable flow model is the primary vehicle; anatomy-labelling, a 3D heart for orientation, and a consolidation quiz are complementary scaffolds.
misconceptions: 'The heart makes blood' — it pumps blood, it does not manufacture it (blood cells are made in bone marrow).
'Blood is just red liquid' — missing that it is a mixture of cells, platelets and plasma, each with a job.
'Arteries are red and veins are blue' — vessels are not coloured; the shorthand refers to oxygen level, and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue. Veins only look blue through skin.
'Blood does one loop around the body' — missing the double circuit; children often think blood goes heart→body→heart and forget the separate lung trip to reload oxygen.
'The heart is on the left and heart-shaped' — it sits centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, and is a fist-sized muscular pump, not the symbolic shape.
'Capillaries are just tiny tubes' — missing that their one-cell-thick walls are the whole point: they are WHERE exchange happens.

activities.title: Drive the double loop and follow one drop
steps: Tap or hold a beating-heart control so a drop of blood advances around the whole circuit: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body → repeat.
Watch the blood flush bright red as it passes the lungs and darken as it threads the body's capillaries.
Turn on a 'follow one drop' option that locks the view onto a single cell for its full body → heart → lung → heart → body journey, and say out loud where it reloads and where it unloads oxygen.
Speed up the beat and notice delivery quickens, then link this to why exercise raises heart rate.
Trace the complete loop aloud, repeatedly, so it is experienced as one continuous circuit rather than a labelled diagram.
activities.insight: Blood must pass through the lungs to turn bright red (pick up oxygen) before going round the body again. In humans it then comes back to the heart to be pumped hard out to the body, so the circuit is two loops through the heart: heart → lungs → heart, then heart → body → heart. The same blood keeps circulating; it is never used up.

activities.title: Name the parts in context: heart cutaway and 'jar of blood'
steps: On a four-chamber heart cutaway, tap each chamber and say its job: atria receive (fill), ventricles push (pump).

Tap each vessel type in the flowing context and state its function: artery carries blood away from the heart (feel the pulse as it pushes), vein carries blood back with valves, capillary is the too-small-to-see meeting point where exchange happens — in the body's tissues oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected, while in the lungs it is the other way round.

Explore a 'jar of blood' separation showing the four components in three layers — plasma on top, a thin layer of white cells and platelets together, red cells at the bottom — and match each component to its job (red: carry oxygen; white: fight infection; platelets: clotting; plasma: the liquid that carries everything).
Keep 'what blood is made of' as a separate step from 'where blood goes': build the four-part composition first, then set that mixture moving through the loop.
activities.insight: The named parts each have a function matched to their structure — capillaries' one-cell-thick walls are the whole point (that is WHERE exchange happens), not merely tiny tubes.

activities.title: Feel your own pump: pulse and the body as manipulative
steps: Find the pulse in your wrist or neck and feel it push — this is an artery.
Point out the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand: these are veins seen through the skin (the blood inside is not blue).
Measure your resting pulse by counting beats over a set time.
Do some brisk activity, measure the pulse again, and explain why a faster pump means more oxygen delivered to the body.
Locate where the heart really sits — centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, about fist-sized — not on the far left and not the symbolic heart shape.
activities.insight: The pulse is the felt heartbeat driving blood through an artery; when the body needs more oxygen the pump speeds up to deliver it, previewing how circulation and breathing work together.

activities.title: Brief 3D orientation: what shape and where the heart really is
steps: Briefly view a 3D heart to see it is a chunky central muscle, not a flat symbolic shape, and to see its real position in the chest.
State in your own words where the heart sits and roughly how big it is.
activities.insight: The real heart is a fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally behind the breastbone, correcting the symbolic 'heart shape on the left' picture.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sequence, match, categorise
steps: Put the double-loop stages in order: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.
Match each vessel type to its function (artery / vein / capillary).
Categorise the four blood components (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) by their jobs.
Answer the reasoning prompt: what would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
activities.insight: Sequencing, matching and categorising can confirm the named parts are recalled and connected to the reason the lung trip must come before the body trip; but these checks test recall, so they do not by themselves build the flow intuition.

checkQuestion: Blood leaves your heart, and later the very same blood comes back to your heart again. Why does it need to make TWO different trips — one to your lungs and one to the rest of your body — instead of just one loop around? Explain what the blood picks up or drops off on each trip.
checkAnswer: Blood makes a double loop. On the trip to the lungs it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen; it returns to the heart, which pumps it out again on the second trip to the body, where it delivers oxygen and nutrients to the cells and collects their carbon-dioxide waste; then it returns to the heart to be sent to the lungs again. Two loops are needed so the blood is re-oxygenated at the lungs before being sent round the body — and the blood keeps returning, it is never used up.
